chapter_title: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
learning_objective: The learner will classify twelve classroom tasks into the six levels of the 2001 revised Bloom's Taxonomy, correctly placing at least ten of twelve on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** bloom-level-task-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify twelve classroom tasks into the six levels of the 2001 revised Bloom's Taxonomy, correctly placing at least ten of twelve on the first attempt. **Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/bloom-taxonomy
**Prerequisites:** Bloom's Taxonomy, the six levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create), learning outcome, higher-order thinking (all defined in the section "Bloom's Taxonomy and Higher-Order Thinking" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns each of the 12 tasks to one of six level bins and submits it. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading level descriptions and hovering over bins is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) The verb alone decides the level (for example, any task containing "explain" must be Understand). (2) Harder or longer tasks are always at higher levels. (3) Writing anything is automatically Create. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying is an Understand-level skill: the learner must recognize which level definition fits an unfamiliar task and commit to an answer before seeing feedback. Mixing subjects prevents the learner from sorting by topic instead of by kind of thinking. **Content:** Six bins, in this order, each with its one-line definition shown on request: | Bin | Definition shown | |---|---| | Remember | Retrieve facts and terms from memory | | Understand | Explain ideas in your own words | | Apply | Use a procedure or idea in a given situation | | Analyze | Break material into parts and see how they relate | | Evaluate | Make judgments against criteria | | Create | Put elements together into something new | Twelve tasks: | # | Task shown to the learner | Correct level | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | List the planets in order from the Sun. | Remember | The learner only retrieves a memorized sequence. | | 2 | State the year the U.S. Constitution was signed. | Remember | Recalling a single fact is retrieval, even though it is a history task. | | 3 | Explain in your own words why ice floats on water. | Understand | Restating an idea in one's own words shows comprehension, not a new use of it. | | 4 | Summarize the main argument of a newspaper editorial in three sentences. | Understand | Summarizing condenses meaning without judging or restructuring it. | | 5 | Use the area formula to find how much paint is needed to cover a 3 m by 4 m wall. | Apply | A known procedure is carried out in a given situation. | | 6 | Conjugate five new regular -ar verbs in the Spanish preterite tense. | Apply | A learned rule is applied to new cases; nothing is analyzed or invented. | | 7 | Compare two accounts of the same battle and identify where they disagree. | Analyze | The learner breaks two sources into parts and examines how they relate. | | 8 | Break a persuasive speech into its claims, its evidence, and its emotional appeals. | Analyze | Separating a whole into its structural parts is analysis. | | 9 | Judge which of two experiment designs better tests whether fertilizer increases plant growth, and defend your choice. | Evaluate | The learner makes and justifies a judgment against a criterion (a fair test). | | 10 | Score a classmate's essay with the class rubric and justify each score. | Evaluate | Applying criteria to reach a defended judgment is evaluation. | | 11 | Design an experiment to test whether background music affects reaction time. | Create | The learner produces an original plan that did not exist before. | | 12 | Write an original short story that uses foreshadowing. | Create | The learner composes a new work, not a summary or analysis of an existing one. | **Provenance:** Bin definitions are from the chapter section "Bloom's Taxonomy and Higher-Order Thinking," which follows Anderson and Krathwohl (2001). Tasks are illustrative, written for this sim. **Rules:** Each task has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A task is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 12. Mastery is a score >= 10. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one task at a time and the six bins. 2. The learner places the task in a bin and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown. 4. The next task appears. After all 12, the learner sees the score and a list of any misplaced tasks with their correct levels. 5. The learner should notice that tasks 3 and 7 both involve explaining or comparing, yet sit at different levels, and that task 2 is short but still Remember while task 12 is a writing task at Create. **Feedback:** 12 tasks, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct — [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the task counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 12" is shown. Final message for a score >= 10: "You can classify tasks by the kind of thinking they ask for." For a score < 10: "Review the level definitions and try again; the tasks will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Task 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the six empty bins and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 12." The prompt reads "What kind of thinking does this task ask for?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names six levels in the order Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create. The chapter states that higher-order thinking means the top three levels. The objective's mastery bar is 10 of 12.
